scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is named after Osman Taka, a 19th-century Cham Albanian guerrilla leader from Konispol who fought against Ottoman forces.
Folk tradition states that Taka was sentenced to death in Yanina and, upon requesting to dance as his final wish, performed so impressively that his executioners spared him.
on_screen: Map: Albania · Europe
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed at national occasions in Albania and is a core part of the Cham Albanian musical repertoire.
It symbolizes the strength and centrality of the lead dancer and serves as a historical commemoration of the resistance figure Osman Taka.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed in a row with dancers holding hands and elbows bent at 90 degrees.
The lead dancer performs complex steps before dropping to his knees to arch his back and chest, forming a bridge.
The other dancers then step onto the lead dancer's stomach to continue the dance.
Watch for The Bridge.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is accompanied by an ensemble including lute, violin, tambourine, and clarinet, often with vocal accompaniment.
The rhythm follows a 2/4 meter with a 'slow-quick-quick' step pattern.
Listen for the lute, violin, tambourine, clarinet.
The pulse is 2/4.
A lively, rhythmic folk sound driven by the interplay of clarinet and strings, maintaining a steady, driving pulse suitable for a row dance.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Osman Taka, a 19th-century Cham Albanian guerrilla fighter.
In Albania, it is known as 'Vallja Çame e Osman Takës'.
It is a variation of the older Çamçe dance and shares stylistic similarities with the Arvanitiko and Tsamiko dances.
